what_its_for: Hydrocortisone is a steroid medicine used to treat many conditions. It helps reduce swelling, redness, itching, and inflammation. Doctors use it for conditions like low adrenal gland function (Addison's disease), severe allergic reactions, asthma, arthritis, certain skin conditions like eczema and psoriasis, and other inflammatory or immune system problems. The cream or ointment form is used directly on the skin for rashes, insect bites, and itching.
how_to_take: Take the tablet form by mouth with food or milk to help prevent stomach upset. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. If you are using the cream, lotion, or ointment, wash your hands before and after applying it. Apply a thin layer to the affected skin area and gently rub it in. Do not cover the area with a bandage or tight clothing unless your doctor tells you to. Do not use the skin cream in your eyes, mouth, or inside your nose. If you are given an injection, it will be given by a healthcare provider in a clinic or hospital setting.
dosing: Your dose depends on your condition, your weight, and how you respond to the medicine. For adults taking tablets, the typical dose is 20 to 240 mg per day, divided into doses taken 2 to 4 times daily. Your doctor will prescribe the lowest dose that works for you. For skin creams or ointments, apply a thin layer to the affected area 2 to 4 times daily, or as directed by your doctor. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions. Never take more or less than prescribed without asking your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are not sure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist for advice. Never stop taking hydrocortisone suddenly without talking to your doctor, especially if you have been taking it for more than a few weeks, as this can cause serious side effects.
storage: Store hydrocortisone tablets at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Store skin creams and ointments at room temperature and keep the cap tightly closed. Keep all forms of this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Do not use the medicine past the expiration date printed on the label. Properly dispose of any unused or expired medicine — ask your pharmacist how to safely throw it away.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking hydrocortisone, as it can increase the risk of stomach bleeding and ulcers. Avoid close contact with people who have infections like chickenpox, measles, or the flu, because this medicine can weaken your immune system and make it easier for you to get sick. Do not get any live vaccines (such as the live flu nasal spray or yellow fever vaccine) while taking this medicine without checking with your doctor first. Avoid prolonged exposure to sunlight and tanning beds when using the skin cream, as it may make your skin more sensitive. Do not use the skin cream on broken, infected, or severely irritated skin unless instructed by your doctor.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or get emergency help if you experience: sudden weight gain or swelling in your hands, feet, or ankles; severe stomach pain, black or bloody stools, or vomiting blood; vision problems or eye pain; signs of high blood sugar such as increased thirst, frequent urination, or blurred vision; signs of low potassium such as muscle weakness or irregular heartbeat; signs of infection such as fever, chills, or sore throat that won't go away; mood changes, depression, or feeling confused; unusual bruising or slow wound healing; or a severe allergic reaction including hives, swelling of the face, lips, or throat, or difficulty breathing. Also call your doctor if you are under unusual stress (such as surgery or illness), as your dose may need to be adjusted.
when_it_works: For inflammation and allergic reactions, you may start to feel better within a few hours to a day or two of starting hydrocortisone. For skin conditions, the itching and redness may begin to improve within a few days of using the cream or ointment. Full improvement may take 1 to 2 weeks depending on your condition. For long-term conditions like adrenal gland problems, you will need to take this medicine every day as a replacement for hormones your body does not make enough of. Do not stop taking it just because you feel better — always follow your doctor's instructions.
special_populations: Older adults (65 and over): You may be more sensitive to the side effects of hydrocortisone, including bone thinning (osteoporosis), high blood pressure, and increased blood sugar. Your doctor will monitor you carefully and use the lowest effective dose. Children: This medicine can slow growth in children when used for a long time. The doctor will check your child's growth regularly. Use the skin cream sparingly in children and only as directed by the doctor. Pregnant women: Talk to your doctor before using hydrocortisone if you are pregnant. It should only be used if clearly needed. Breastfeeding women: Small amounts of this medicine can pass into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding while on this medicine. People with diabetes: Hydrocortisone can raise blood sugar levels. Monitor your blood sugar more closely and report any changes to your doctor. People with osteoporosis: Long-term use can weaken bones. Ask your doctor about calcium and vitamin D supplements to help protect your bones.
